content_html:
A HELOC works like a credit card with your house as collateral: the lender sets a borrowing limit and you draw on it as you need. During the draw period, often 10 years, you can borrow as needed and usually only have to pay interest. When the draw period ends, the repayment period begins: you can no longer borrow, and the balance is paid off with principal and interest over the remaining years. Most HELOCs have a variable rate. This calculator shows the credit line you might qualify for, the payments in each phase, and how sensitive those payments are to rate changes.

How to use this calculator

  1. Home value and mortgage balance: a recent estimate of what your home would sell for, and what you still owe on any existing mortgages.
  2. Combined loan-to-value limit: the share of the home's value a lender will let all loans add up to. 80% to 90% is common.
  3. Amount, rate and periods: how much you plan to use, the current HELOC rate, and the lengths of the draw and repayment periods from the offer.
  4. When you draw: all at once, as for a single project, or in equal monthly amounts, as for ongoing costs.
  5. More options: extra principal during the draw period, closing costs and any annual fee.

How it is calculated

The credit line is home value × CLTV limit − mortgage balance. During the draw period each month's payment is the interest on the balance, the balance times the yearly rate divided by 12, plus any extra principal. When the draw period ends, the remaining balance is repaid with the standard formula P = B × i / (1 − (1 + i)−n), where n is the number of repayment months. The rate table reruns the same plan with the rate 1, 2 and 3 points higher.

A worked example

A home worth $450,000 with a $250,000 mortgage has $200,000 of equity. At an 80% limit, a lender would allow total loans of $360,000, so the line could be up to $110,000. Drawing $50,000 at the start at 8.5%, with a 10-year draw period and a 20-year repayment period:

PhaseMonthly payment at 8.5%At 10.5%
Draw period (interest only)$354.17$437.50
Repayment period$433.91$499.19

The payment rises by $79.74, about 23%, the month repayment starts, and total interest over 30 years is $96,638.79. Drawing the same $50,000 in equal monthly amounts over the draw period lowers total interest to $75,565.87, because the balance is smaller for most of those years.

Tips for using a HELOC

  • Plan for the repayment jump. Paying some principal during the draw period, even a small fixed amount, lowers the balance and softens the increase.
  • Stress-test the rate. If a 2- or 3-point rise would strain your budget, borrow less or look at a fixed-rate home equity loan.
  • Check the costs. Ask about closing costs, annual fees, early closure fees and minimum draw requirements, and whether part of the balance can be locked at a fixed rate.
  • Know the tax rule. Interest is generally deductible only when the money is used to buy, build or substantially improve the home that secures the loan, and only if you itemize.
  • Remember the collateral. Your home secures the line, so missed payments can lead to foreclosure, and a lender can freeze or reduce the line if your home's value falls.

Limits of this estimate

Real HELOCs charge interest daily on the average balance, may have rate caps or floors, and set their own minimum payments, so your statements will differ somewhat. The credit line is an estimate only: the lender's appraisal, your credit and your income decide the actual amount.

faq.question: What is the difference between a HELOC and a home equity loan?
faq.answer: A home equity loan pays you a lump sum at a fixed rate with fixed payments from the start. A HELOC is a revolving line you draw on as needed, usually at a variable rate, with interest-only payments during the draw period.

faq.question: Can I pay off a HELOC early?
faq.answer: Usually, yes. You can repay principal at any time during the draw period and borrow it again. Some lenders charge an early closure fee if you close the line within the first few years, so check the agreement.

faq.question: What happens when the draw period ends?
faq.answer: You can no longer borrow, and the balance converts to a repayment schedule with principal and interest. Some lines instead require the full balance as a balloon payment, so confirm which applies to yours.

faq.question: How do HELOC rates change?
faq.answer: Most HELOC rates are the prime rate plus a fixed margin, so they rise and fall when the prime rate moves, typically after Federal Reserve rate changes. Your agreement lists the margin and any caps.

faq.question: Does opening a HELOC affect my credit?
faq.answer: The application usually involves a hard credit inquiry, and the new account and its balance appear on your credit report. Using a large share of the line can affect your score, as can on-time or late payments.
